beats.text: count plus plus broke because load and store were separate steps. What if the hardware did it all in one?
test and set does. In one atomic step, it returns the old value of the lock, and sets the lock to true.
A process spins while test and set returns true. When it returns false, the lock was free, and now it is held.
Leaving, the process sets the lock back to false.
Programmers use a friendlier tool built on top: the mutex lock. Acquire before the critical section. Release after.
Five threads, each doing count plus plus inside the lock. The count always ends at five.
If waiting means looping, the lock is a spinlock. The waiting thread burns CPU doing nothing.
A semaphore is an integer, S, touched only by two atomic operations: wait, and signal.
Think of S as the number of free resources. Here, three.
wait takes one. One, two, three processes take one each. S is zero.
A fourth calls wait. S drops to minus one, and it sleeps in the semaphore's queue. A negative S counts the sleepers.
When a process calls signal, S goes up by one, and one sleeper wakes.
A semaphore that is only zero or one works like a mutex. The difference: a mutex has an owner. Only the thread that locked it may unlock it.
Semaphores can also force an order. Start synch at zero. P two calls wait, and sleeps.
P one runs S one, then signals. Only now can P two run S two. S one always comes first.
But locks can trap you. P zero takes S, then Q. P one takes Q, then S.
Each holds one lock, and waits for the other's. Neither lets go. That is deadlock.
The fix: take the locks in the same order everywhere.
Two more failures. Starvation: one process never gets its turn. Priority inversion: a low priority process holds a lock that a high priority one needs.
